explanations.explanation: Close, baker, but the message says the opposite. It says, "Do not rejoice, all you Philistines, that the rod that struck you is broken." (Isaiah 14:29) So the Philistines are told not to celebrate. I know a broken rod sounds like a party, but the message hands them a reason to hold the confetti.

Right, the message says, "Do not rejoice, all you Philistines, that the rod that struck you is broken." (Isaiah 14:29) It tells them not to rejoice. A broken rod sounds like cake and balloons, but the message has more to say. Keep that confetti in the closet, friend.

You've got it, baker. The message says, "a viper will spring from the root of the snake, and a flying serpent from its egg." (Isaiah 14:29) So the snake's root isn't done producing trouble. A viper is a venomous snake, and a flying serpent comes right behind it. That is a LOT of snake news for one verse.

A lion is a solid guess, friend, since lions are famous for being scary. But the message stays with snakes here. It says, "a viper will spring from the root of the snake, and a flying serpent from its egg." (Isaiah 14:29) The answer is a viper, and a flying serpent follows it.

A bear would make me nervous too, baker. But the message keeps this one in the snake family. It says, "a viper will spring from the root of the snake, and a flying serpent from its egg." (Isaiah 14:29) So the answer is a viper, and no bears are invited.

That's right, baker. The message says, "Then the firstborn of the poor will find pasture, and the needy will lie down in safety." (Isaiah 14:30) Pasture for the poor and safety for the needy. Lying down in safety sounds like the best nap of my life, and I've napped in a drawer.

Not quite, friend. The message says, "Then the firstborn of the poor will find pasture, and the needy will lie down in safety." (Isaiah 14:30) So the needy get safety along with the pasture. Both of those are in the verse, and I'm happy about it.

Yes, baker. The message says, "I will kill your root by famine." (Isaiah 14:30) It is a hard line, and I won't joke about it. The root is what a plant grows from, and here it is the Philistines' root that is named.

I see why fire comes to mind, friend, but that isn't the word here. The message says, "I will kill your root by famine." (Isaiah 14:30) So the answer is famine. This is a heavy line, and the text says it plainly.

Plague is a heavy word, baker, but it isn't the one in this verse. The message says, "I will kill your root by famine." (Isaiah 14:30) So the answer is famine. It's a hard line, so we just read it carefully.

Careful, baker, the verse goes the other way. It says, "I will kill your root by famine, and your remnant will be slain." (Isaiah 14:30) So the remnant is not spared. It's a hard line, and it takes a careful read to catch it.

That's right, baker. The message says, "I will kill your root by famine, and your remnant will be slain." (Isaiah 14:30) So the remnant is not spared. This is a heavy verse, and it's good to read it slowly.

You've got it, baker. The message says, "a cloud of smoke comes from the north." (Isaiah 14:31) The gate and the city are told to wail because of it. Smoke on the horizon is a sight nobody wants to see, and I'd wail a little too.
Good guess, friend, but this one points the other way. The message says, "a cloud of smoke comes from the north." (Isaiah 14:31) So the answer is north. Time to turn the compass around.
West is a fair guess, baker, but the verse says otherwise. It says, "a cloud of smoke comes from the north." (Isaiah 14:31) So the answer is north. Spin that compass one more time and you're there.

Yes, baker. The message says, "there are no stragglers in its ranks." (Isaiah 14:31) Nobody is lagging behind in that line. I could never keep my cookie cutters in a line that straight on the counter, so I'm impressed.
Not this time, friend. The message says, "there are no stragglers in its ranks." (Isaiah 14:31) So nobody is falling behind in that cloud of smoke. Every single one keeps up.

That's it, baker. The answer is, "The LORD has founded Zion, where His afflicted people will find refuge." (Isaiah 14:32) Refuge is a safe place to run to. After the wailing in this passage, it is good to end on that.

Riches sound lovely, friend, but the verse promises something else. It says, "The LORD has founded Zion, where His afflicted people will find refuge." (Isaiah 14:32) So the answer is refuge, a safe place for the afflicted. I'd take that over a pile of gold any day.

Power is a fair guess, baker, but it isn't the word in the verse. It says, "The LORD has founded Zion, where His afflicted people will find refuge." (Isaiah 14:32) So the answer is refuge. That's a safe place, and the afflicted are the ones who find it.
